rationale: A wins because it knows where the story ends and the fact-check begins: "confirm it is live today rather than announced for later" is exactly the guardrail this launch needs. B has usable bones, but "live in 50 countries at once, not a phased pilot" and "Brex spends big on global infrastructure" manufacture certainty and cost pressure the update did not supply. That is not strategy; that is handing a reporter the loose thread.
gaps_in_A: "The finance team that stopped wiring reimbursements across borders" turns a plausible before-state into fact. The update says local reimbursement, not that customers were wiring reimbursements before.

"How Brex built card issuing and local-currency reimbursement in 50 countries" is a good infrastructure angle, but it depends almost entirely on Brex disclosing partners, licenses, settlement, and FX mechanics. Without that, it is an interview wish list.
"Enterprise customers pushed Brex, the startup card company, to go global" needs proof that the market still sees Brex primarily as a startup-card company, not just a customer-mix fact.
gaps_in_B: "cards and local-currency reimbursement live in 50 countries at once, not a phased pilot" is invented. The update says launching in 50 countries; it does not say live everywhere at once.
"announced today" and "live today" are asserted repeatedly. The supplied timestamp is not the same as a confirmed announcement date or go-live status.
"Brex spends big on global infrastructure without saying if it's profitable" invents spending magnitude and turns undisclosed profitability into a financial-health story without evidence.
Refusing a customer story as "hallucinated_fact" is too rigid. A named customer was not supplied, but a customer-led angle is valid if the next proof item is exactly to find one.
